t: Why You Must Never Confuse Fun And Hard Work https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2015/09/26/why-you-must-never-confuse-fun-and-hard-work/
q: Fun is merely a tool. Although real and wonderful, it’s a tool that opens the door to learning. It isn’t learning itself—at least, it shouldn’t be most of the time.
You see, the danger in trying to make every lesson an inflatable bounce house is that you send the message that if it isn’t fun, then it doesn’t have value and therefore isn’t worth doing.
With excessive television, video games, text messaging, social media, and the like conspiring to shorten attention spans and weaken observational power, we must provide the counterpoint.
Your job is to provide world-class instruction, to emote, mimic, and dramatize, to bring the curriculum to life for your students . . . and then turn responsibility over to them.
Although our students come to us with varying levels of attentiveness, they can all improve. The idea that they have a fixed ability of which we can do little about is hogwash.
But the rewards are no less than a productive, well-behaved class who can’t wait to get to school every day.
x: Fun and humor are valuable tools that open the door to learning, but they must not be mistaken for learning itself.

Linsin affirms his belief in bringing genuine fun, humor, and dynamic teaching into the classroom, but warns against a growing danger: treating fun as the goal itself rather than as a tool that opens the door to serious…
He rejects the idea that students have a fixed capacity for attentiveness, insisting instead that stamina for hard work can and must be deliberately built.
The reward for this balance, he writes, is a productive, engaged class that is genuinely transformed by the end of the year.

t: Why You Should Never Punish Your Entire Class For The Behavior Of A Few ass-for-the-behavior-of-a-few/
q: The problem with the strategy, however, is that it alienates your most well-behaved students.
Students from kindergarten on up have an acute sense of fairness. Although they may not always voice their frustration to you, you can bet they’ll bring it up at the dinner table.
First, you should never redo a routine if the problem is just a few students.
Also, when you redo a routine, it’s not because of misbehavior. It’s because your class did the routine incorrectly.
Finally, when you ask students to repeat a routine, you’re not taking anything away from them. They aren’t missing recess or arriving late to lunch or losing out on class points.

To sum up, when individual students misbehave, hold them accountable individually by following your classroom management plan . If it’s more than one or two at a time, then it’s a sign you must become a more vigilant observer.

t: Why Giving A “Look” Is A Poor Classroom Management Strategy agement-strategy/
q: Whenever you glare at students, or otherwise try to intimidate them into behaving, you create a you-against-them relationship.

You make it personal. You give the impression that not only are you angry, but you dislike them personally. After all, when someone gives a dirty look, that’s the natural conclusion—especially with children.
When you give a “look,” you have no way of knowing whether your students understand what it means. They may not even be sure you’re looking at them or what behavior you’re referring to.
When you promise to follow your classroom management plan, but then go back on your word and glare instead, you send the message that you can’t be trusted.
But now Robert can’t stand his teacher and has little motivation to push himself academically.
You must follow your classroom management plan as its written and give them an opportunity to take responsibility all on their own—without your dirty looks, lectures, or two cents.
x: Giving students a silent 'look' to curb misbehavior may work momentarily but damages long-term teacher-student relationships.
He identifies the practice as antagonistic, since it creates a personal, adversarial dynamic and communicates dislike rather than impersonal accountability.

It's also confusing, he notes, because students often can't be sure what behavior triggered the look or even whether it was directed at them, undermining the clarity effective classroom management requires.
Using intimidation instead of a stated classroom management plan is a form of inconsistency that undermines trust.

t: How To Handle Needy, Grabby, Dependent Students udents/
q: When you lean down toward needy students, you encourage their behavior. You encourage more drama and more interruptions in the future.
In the immediate moments following their interruption, it’s important that you don’t respond. It’s okay to look in their direction to let them know you hear them, but refrain from opening your mouth.
Give them a chance to catch themselves, to rethink their behavior, to consider a more mature and polite way of speaking to you.
This tendency will only worsen if you validate their behavior. It will only worsen if you stop what you’re doing, allow them to interrupt you, and show concern.
The level of dependency in your classroom is directly related to how you respond to it.
They will turn your students into doers and problem-solvers, independent learners and lean-in listeners. They will build confidence and competence and even strengthen character.
